name: Tessen Colony
desc: A struggling farm colony beyond patrol range. They have food, and they have a problem.

gm.feel: Turned earth, woodsmoke and the burnt-sugar smell of grain drying in sheds, under a real sky that makes fleet people dizzy. Everything has been mended at least twice, and nobody hurries or waves. You don't buy from Tessen: you work beside them till they've decided about you, and then a price comes out in bushels and a handshake, and it's never written down because nobody here would need it to be.

districts.name: The Commons
districts.desc: The grain sheds, the meeting barn and the marshal's one-room office, around a square of packed dirt. Elder Dray holds council on an upturned feed trough.

districts.name: The Long Fields
districts.desc: Forty kilometers of grain on land no one thought would ever grow any. Yields have been the best in thirty years, for the last two years, in the north section.

districts.name: The Well-Head
districts.desc: A new well in the north section, capped in poured stone and fenced off with a sign that says DRY. It isn't dry, and the stone stays warm in frost.

districts.name: The Schoolhouse
districts.desc: Forty-one children and one tired teacher, in a building that smells of chalk and boots. Something's been drawn on the floor under the desks, and it keeps coming back after it's scrubbed.

districts.name: The Far Homesteads
districts.desc: Isolated farms a day's ride out, where people are stubborn, armed and often the last to hear anything. Raiders hit these first.

complications: A raider scouting party has been seen on the ridge, and half the colony thinks your ship brought them.
Refugees from your fleet have started trading illegally with the outlying farms, and someone's been cheated.
A child in your party's care starts speaking fluently in the language nobody knows.
A dust storm grounds your shuttle at a far homestead, with people who hate uniforms and have every reason to.
Elder Dray learns exactly how bad things really are, in front of a crowd, from you.
Harvest is three days off, and the blight's reached the south fields. The north fields are untouched, and nobody wants to say why.
secrets: Marshal Dey has told Elder Dray that six children are affected. The real number is thirty-one, nearly every child under twelve, and her own son was the first. They walk out to the Well-Head in their sleep, all at the same hour, and she and the teacher carry them back before dawn. The stone cap has cracked from below twice.

The warm chamber under the Well-Head is a First Builder school that has woken up, and it's training replacements. Its warmth is also behind the north fields' wonderful yield. The grain is safe to eat, as far as anyone can test, and a little of it has already gone to the fleet.

The children's language is First Builder, and they're its only living speakers. When they speak it to each other, and in the turns of their skipping game, they're practicing one long phrase. It's doing them no harm, so far.

encounters: Elder Dray hands you a hoe before you've finished saying who you are. Folk who want to talk, she says, can talk working. A row later, you notice that the entire village is pretending not to watch how you handle it.

Marshal Sorrel Dey's only deputy is an old dog. She pours you something awful in her office and asks, plainly, that if you speak to the Elder you say six children. She won't tell you what the real number is unless you ask her twice.

A seven-year-old sitting on a fence says something long and musical to you in a language you've never heard. Then she adds in plain speech that you don't have to write it down, because the other one's going to. There's nobody else there.

A mother has moved her son into the root cellar to sleep, so that the neighbors can't hear him at night. She needs medicine she doesn't want to name, and she'd like you to forget where you bought the eggs.

An old homesteader meets you on the road with a rifle and tries to pay his forty years of back taxes to the Concord, in turnips, out of pure spite. He's got them loaded on a cart. It's a great many turnips, and your fleet is hungry.

A farmer offers you thirty tons of grain, and he's not asking for credits. All his sons went off with the Concord navy, and he wants ten strong refugees for five growing seasons. They'd be fed and treated decently. He has a contract, and it's written in crayon.

A family from your fleet has walked off the shuttle and refuses to go back. They've sat down at the edge of the field and started pulling weeds. Dray has told you no more mouths, and she's walking over now.

A raider boy of about fourteen has been caught stealing seed. Old Tessen law says he goes out past the fence with no water. Dey says she won't do it, Dray says she will, and the crowd says you might take him off everyone's hands.

The well-digger who found the chamber won't touch well water any more, and he drinks only from his rain barrels. He presses a sealed jar on you and asks you to take it to a real doctor. He hasn't told anyone that he's been leaving his own bread at the stone.

The teacher takes you into the empty schoolhouse and rolls back the rug. It's the same chalk drawing the children have made every night for a month, and she thinks it's a map. Your navigator would be able to tell you which way up it goes.

It's the harvest fair, and you've been asked to judge the pie contest. All three bakers have been feuding for decades, the winner's family gets first choice of seed rights for the year, and each has already told you what the others put in the crust.

A courteous Hegemony surveyor has set up a little tent by the north fields, taking soil samples. His papers are in perfect order, and his offer to the colony is generous: free medical care for all the children, in return for a small monthly report.

A very old woman keeps the key to the Concord seed vault on a string around her neck, and she's been told by nobody to give it to anybody. She'd like to know whether you plan to plant what's in there or eat it. She's already heard your people are starving, so she'd like you to think before you answer.

You can't sleep under a real sky, so you go for a walk, and at four in the morning you meet Marshal Dey and the schoolteacher coming down the north road. Each of them is carrying a sleeping child, and there's a long line of small footprints in the frost behind them. Neither of them says anything. Dey shifts the boy on her shoulder and looks at you.

A boy from your fleet and a girl from Tessen have fallen in love over a broken harvester. She wants to leave with him, and he wants to stay. Her father wants to know what your intentions are, because he thinks you're the boy's commanding officer, and you sort of are.
rumors: Ground's warm in the north forty, right through the middle of winter. Best yield I've seen in thirty years, and I'm not saying I wouldn't eat it. I'm saying I've been eating from the south.

My gran's gran used to talk about the silver visitors, who'd come and sit up with the dying and be gone by morning. That's an old story, older than the Concord. I don't know why nobody wants to hear it now.
Elder Dray says a seed planted in anger comes up crooked. She also says she's fired that rifle just the once. I wouldn't ask who at.
Kids round here have a new skipping game. Goes on for hours, and they never drop a beat. You try and get them to teach it to you, and they look at you like you're the sick one.
The marshal's a good woman, and she's never told me a lie, and I'd like you to think about how I said that.

Word from the far farms is that raiders have stopped taking grain, and they've started taking children's schoolbooks. It's a daft story. My neighbor swears to it, and he's never had an idea in his life.
Don't drive your cart past the stone at the new well, it spooks the horses. It doesn't spook the kids any. You'll see a dozen of them out there at dusk, just sat.
There's a Concord seed vault somewhere on this world. Old stock from before they forgot about us. Enough to plant a whole planet, is what the old folks say, if you could find a planet.
Your lot look hungry. We'd feed you, I expect. Thing is, thirty thousand of you and two thousand of us, so you'll understand why I've been cleaning my gun.
We had a fellow from the Hegemony out here saying that the food's better under protection. Told him we'd give it some thought. He's still out there, and he's going to be a long time waiting.
One thing about this place: nobody's ever come out here to help us and stayed to the end of a harvest. I've got a bet going, if you want in.
That teacher's started sleeping at the school. Says it's on account of the roof. There's nothing wrong with the roof.
My youngest asked me the other night why we're all talking so slow. Nobody talks slow here. I mean, we do. But he never asked before.
They say that if you leave a sick animal up near the Well-Head overnight, it's better by morning. I've seen it. I had a sick cow. I've still got a cow, and I don't go in the barn much.
